summary: Paul greets the Corinthian church, thanking God for the grace and gifts they have in Christ. He urgently calls them to unity, rejecting factions around different leaders. Paul contrasts worldly wisdom with the message of the cross, which seems foolish but is God’s power and wisdom. He reminds them that God chose the lowly so that no one may boast, and that Christ is their wisdom, righteousness, holiness, and redemption.
main_themes: The power and wisdom of the cross
Humility and boasting in the Lord

passage_divisions.title: Greeting, Thanksgiving, and Assurance
A Call to Unity, Not Personalities
The Cross and the Folly of Worldly Wisdom
God’s Choice of the Lowly; Boast in the Lord

book_connection: This chapter sets the tone for the letter by addressing disunity and re-centering the church on Christ crucified. It introduces themes that resurface throughout: spiritual gifts, true wisdom, leadership, and humble dependence on God.
jesus_connection: Jesus is the crucified and risen Lord whose cross is God’s power and wisdom. Believers are called into fellowship with Him, and in Him they receive righteousness, holiness, and redemption—leaving no room for boasting in human leaders or abilities.

summary: Paul reminds the Corinthians that he came not with flashy rhetoric but with the simple, saving message of Jesus Christ crucified, confirmed by the Spirit’s power. He contrasts God’s hidden wisdom with the temporary wisdom of the age, explaining that true understanding comes only through the Holy Spirit. Natural thinking finds the gospel foolish, but the Spirit enables believers to discern God’s gifts and to share in the mind of Christ.
main_themes: Christ crucified as true wisdom and power
Dependence on the Holy Spirit for revelation and faith
Contrast between worldly wisdom and God’s wisdom
Spiritual discernment and the mind of Christ

passage_divisions.title: Christ Crucified, Not Human Eloquence
God’s Hidden Wisdom Revealed by the Spirit
Spiritual Discernment and the Mind of Christ

book_connection: This chapter continues 1 Corinthians’ opening emphasis on the cross as God’s true wisdom and the basis of Christian unity. It prepares for later corrections about spiritual maturity, boasting, and spiritual gifts by rooting everything in the Spirit’s work, not human status.
jesus_connection: Jesus is the center: Paul proclaims Christ crucified, the surprising wisdom of God. Through the Spirit, believers participate in Jesus’ mind and gain access to God’s purposes revealed in the gospel.

summary: Paul confronts the Corinthians’ immaturity shown in their divisions over leaders. He reframes ministers like Paul and Apollos as servants, insists that God alone gives growth, and warns that each person’s work will be tested. He reminds the church they are God’s temple, calls them to reject worldly wisdom, and urges them to boast only in Christ because all things are theirs in Him.

passage_divisions.title: Spiritual Infancy and Factionalism
Servants Through Whom You Believed
Building on the Only Foundation
You Are God’s Temple
True Wisdom and All Things Are Yours

book_connection: This chapter continues Paul’s appeal for unity in a divided church (chs. 1–4) by exposing worldly thinking and re-centering everything on Christ. It lays groundwork for later corrections about church life, leadership, and holiness throughout 1 Corinthians.
jesus_connection: Jesus is named as the sole foundation of the church and the one to whom believers belong. The gospel unites diverse people, reorders our values away from worldly status, and promises future evaluation of our works in light of Christ.

summary: Paul urges the Corinthians to view church leaders as Christ’s servants and God’s stewards, accountable to the Lord’s judgment rather than human appraisal. He rebukes their pride with sharp irony, contrasting their self-satisfaction with the apostles’ suffering. As their spiritual father, he calls them to imitate his way of life and sends Timothy to remind them. He warns the arrogant that the kingdom is about power, not talk, and that he can come with discipline or gentleness.

passage_divisions.title: Servants and Stewards, Not Judges
Irony and the Apostolic Pattern of Suffering
A Father’s Appeal: Imitate My Way of Life
Talk or Power? Paul’s Coming Visit

book_connection: This chapter continues Paul’s correction of divisions over leaders (chs. 1–3) by redefining leadership as faithful stewardship and by exposing pride. It prepares for practical discipline and order in the church that follows (chs. 5–6, 11–14).
jesus_connection: Paul frames leaders as servants of Christ and leaves final judgment to the Lord, centering Jesus as Master and Judge. The apostles’ pattern of suffering echoes the way of the cross, showing that gospel ministry bears Christ’s marks and depends on His power.

summary: Paul confronts the Corinthian church for tolerating an incestuous relationship and calls them to act decisively for the offender’s ultimate salvation and the church’s holiness. He uses Passover imagery—Christ our Passover lamb—to urge the removal of moral ‘leaven.’ Paul clarifies that Christians are not to withdraw from the world but must practice loving discipline toward professing believers who persist in serious, unrepentant sin. God judges those outside; the church must address those inside.

passage_divisions.title: A Scandal and a Command to Act
Leaven and the Passover Lamb
Judging Inside, Not Outside

book_connection: After addressing pride and division (chs. 1–4), Paul applies gospel wisdom to a concrete moral crisis. This chapter advances the book’s aim: a cross-shaped community marked by holiness, humility, and love that protects the church’s witness.
jesus_connection: Paul anchors the call to holiness in Jesus: Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed, making the church a new, unleavened people. Discipline aims at salvation through Christ, mirroring Jesus’ own teaching on pursuing a straying brother.

summary: Paul rebukes the Corinthians for taking fellow believers to secular courts and urges them to resolve disputes within the church. He warns that those who persist in unrighteous lifestyles will not inherit God’s kingdom, reminding them of their new identity in Christ. He then corrects distortions of Christian freedom, teaching that the body belongs to the Lord, is destined for resurrection, is a temple of the Holy Spirit, and must be kept from sexual immorality.
main_themes: Union with Christ and sexual holiness

passage_divisions.title: Believers and Lawsuits Before Unbelievers
From Old Life to New Identity
Bodies for the Lord: Freedom, Union, and Purity

book_connection: This chapter continues Paul’s correction of Corinthian pride and divisions (chs. 1–4) and immoral toleration (ch. 5), applying the gospel to conflicts and sexuality. It prepares for later teaching on freedom, love, and the body (chs. 8–10; 12–15).
jesus_connection: Jesus purchased believers with His blood and was bodily raised—truths that ground Paul’s call to honor God with our bodies. Union with Christ reshapes relationships, conflict, and sexuality, displaying the gospel’s transforming power.

summary: Paul answers questions about marriage, singleness, sex, divorce, and life-calling. He urges faithfulness in marriage, honors celibacy as a gift, and counsels believers to remain as they were when called, especially given a present crisis. He addresses mixed marriages with unbelievers, the freedom of widows to remarry in the Lord, and the value of undivided devotion to Christ.
important_people: Corinthian believers (married, single, widowed, slaves, free)

passage_divisions.title: Mutuality in Marriage and Temporary Abstinence
Guidance for Married, Separated, and Mixed-Believer Marriages
Remain as You Were Called (Circumcision, Slavery, Vocation)
Virgins and the Present Crisis
Undivided Devotion: Concerns of Single and Married
Betrothal Decisions
Widowhood and Remarriage in the Lord

book_connection: After confronting sexual immorality (ch. 5–6), Paul gives practical counsel for holy relationships and callings. The chapter advances the letter’s call to wise, loving use of freedom and to live in light of the coming kingdom.
jesus_connection: Jesus taught on marriage, divorce, and singleness for the kingdom. Paul applies Jesus’ lordship to daily decisions—marriage, celibacy, and vocation—so believers can serve Christ with peace and undivided hearts.

summary: Paul answers a question about eating food sacrificed to idols. He teaches that love, not mere knowledge, must guide believers, because some have weak consciences shaped by their past with idols. While idols are nothing and there is only one God and one Lord, Christians must guard their freedom so it doesn’t harm others. Paul concludes that he would gladly give up meat rather than cause a brother or sister to stumble.
main_themes: One God and one Lord (monotheistic confession)

passage_divisions.title: Knowledge vs. Love
One God and One Lord
Freedom, Conscience, and Love’s Restraint

book_connection: This chapter extends Paul’s counsel on unity and holiness in a divided church. It sets up his broader discussion of idolatry and communion in chapters 9–10 and models how the gospel reframes everyday choices.
jesus_connection: Paul’s ethic mirrors Jesus’ self-giving love: using freedom to serve others, not self. The confession of ‘one Lord, Jesus Christ’ places Jesus at the center of creation and redemption, anchoring Christian conduct in who he is.

summary: Paul defends his apostleship and his right to receive material support, yet explains why he has chosen not to use that right in Corinth. He shows how he adapts himself to different groups to win them to Christ and urges disciplined, purposeful living for an imperishable crown. The chapter blends personal testimony, scriptural argument, and athletic imagery to model gospel-centered self-denial.

passage_divisions.title: Paul’s Apostolic Rights Asserted
Biblical Basis for Ministry Support
Choosing Not to Use His Rights
Becoming All Things to Win Some
Run to Win: Discipline for an Imperishable Crown

book_connection: Chapter 9 continues Paul’s response to questions about liberty begun in chapter 8 (food offered to idols) and prepares for chapter 10’s warnings and examples. It shows how love governs freedom and how apostolic example grounds Paul’s exhortations to the Corinthians.
jesus_connection: Paul’s self-giving pattern echoes Jesus, who had rightful glory yet became a servant for our salvation. The chapter centers on the gospel of Christ: those who preach it live by it, shape their lives around it, and pursue others so they might share in its blessings.

summary: Paul warns the Corinthians by recalling Israel’s failures in the wilderness and urges them to flee idolatry. He explains how the Lord’s Supper unites believers with Christ, so they must not mix worship of God with pagan practices. He then gives practical guidance on meat offered to idols, balancing freedom with love for others’ consciences. The chapter ends with a call to do everything for God’s glory and to avoid causing anyone to stumble.

passage_divisions.title: Israel’s Example: Privilege and Peril
Written for Our Warning and Hope
The Lord’s Table vs. Idols
Conscience, Freedom, and Neighbor Love
Do All for God’s Glory

book_connection: First Corinthians addresses divisions, immorality, and confusion about worship and freedom. Chapter 10 ties chapters 8–9 to 11 by showing how love, not mere liberty, must guide believers, especially regarding idolatry and the Lord’s Supper.
jesus_connection: Paul identifies the spiritual rock as Christ and shows the Lord’s Supper as participation in Jesus’ body and blood. Our loyalty belongs to Jesus alone; his saving presence and faithful help make escape from temptation possible.

summary: Paul addresses two problems in Corinthian worship: head coverings and disorder at the Lord’s Supper. He urges practices that honor God’s created order and mutual dependence in the church, and he rebukes selfishness that shames the poor during communion. He then recounts Jesus’ words instituting the Supper and calls for self-examination so gatherings bring grace, not judgment.
main_themes: Mutual dependence of men and women
Unity vs. division in the church

passage_divisions.title: Imitate Christ; Headship, Honor, and Head Coverings
Abuses at the Lord’s Supper
Institution of the Lord’s Supper
Examining Ourselves and Waiting for One Another

book_connection: 1 Corinthians addresses divisions, pride, and disorder in the church. Chapter 11 continues the theme of worship shaped by love and holiness, preparing for chapters 12–14 on spiritual gifts and orderly gatherings.
jesus_connection: Jesus is the model Paul follows and the Lord remembered at the Supper. The chapter centers communion on Jesus’ self-giving death and coming return, calling the church to reflect his sacrificial love and unity.

summary: Paul teaches the Corinthians about spiritual gifts and how the Holy Spirit distributes them for the common good. He uses the metaphor of the human body to show the unity and interdependence of believers. He lists roles God has appointed in the church and urges them to pursue the greater gifts, setting up the way of love in the next chapter.
main_themes: Mutual care in the body of Christ

passage_divisions.title: True Spirituality: Confessing Jesus as Lord
Many Gifts, One Spirit, One Purpose
One Body, Many Members
Appointed Roles and the Greater Way

book_connection: First Corinthians addresses a divided church. Chapter 12 confronts pride and chaos around spiritual gifts by emphasizing unity under the Spirit and prepares for chapter 13’s corrective on love and chapter 14’s order in worship.
jesus_connection: The chapter centers on confessing, “Jesus is Lord,” which is the Spirit’s hallmark. Believers are Christ’s body, continuing His ministry on earth; their diverse gifts serve His lordship and witness to the gospel’s unifying power.

summary: Paul pauses his discussion of spiritual gifts to show that love is the essential way of the Christian life. Without love, even the greatest gifts or sacrifices amount to nothing. He then defines love’s character and contrasts its permanence with the temporary nature of gifts, pointing to the maturity and clarity that will come when the perfect arrives.
main_themes: Supremacy of love over spiritual gifts
Partial knowledge now vs. future fullness

passage_divisions.title: Gifts Without Love Are Empty
What Love Is (and Is Not)
Love’s Permanence and Our Future Maturity

book_connection: In a letter correcting divisions and misuse of gifts (chapters 12–14), this chapter is the heart: the “most excellent way.” It reframes all church life and service under love, preparing readers to pursue gifts in an orderly, edifying way.
jesus_connection: Jesus perfectly embodies this love in His life, death, and resurrection. The chapter points to the gospel by showing that love—revealed supremely at the cross—is the enduring mark of God’s people and the measure of true spirituality.

summary: Paul contrasts uninterpreted tongues with intelligible prophecy, urging love-driven use of gifts that build up the church. He gives practical instructions for orderly gatherings, so that believers are edified and unbelievers are convicted. He grounds these directions in God’s character as a God of peace and calls the church to test and submit to apostolic instruction.

passage_divisions.title: Pursue love; prioritize prophecy for edification
Intelligibility illustrated and applied
Signs, conviction, and the outsider
Order in gathered worship
Women, speech, and submission in the assembly
Recognizing the Lord’s command; final summary

book_connection: Chapters 12–14 address spiritual gifts: their diversity (12), their governing way of love (13), and their orderly, edifying use (14). This chapter lands the plane with concrete guidance for Corinth’s chaotic gatherings.
jesus_connection: Jesus builds His church by His Spirit, who gives gifts for the body’s good. Intelligible word-ministry reflects Jesus’ own mission to reveal the Father clearly and to bring peace, not confusion.

summary: Paul reminds the Corinthians of the core gospel—Christ’s death, burial, resurrection, and appearances—and insists the resurrection is essential to Christian faith. He explains the order of resurrection, Christ’s reign over every enemy including death, addresses questions about the resurrection body, and celebrates the final victory over death. The chapter ends with a call to steadfast, hopeful labor in the Lord.
main_themes: Christ’s reign and victory over death

passage_divisions.title: The Gospel of First Importance
If No Resurrection—Then What?
Firstfruits and the End of Death
Why Risk Anything If There’s No Resurrection?
What Kind of Body? From Seed to Splendor
The Final Transformation and Sure Victory

book_connection: First Corinthians addresses church health in doctrine and practice. Chapter 15 anchors everything in the resurrection, correcting confusion and grounding holiness, unity, and mission in the living Christ.
jesus_connection: This chapter centers on Jesus’ death and resurrection as the heart of the gospel, the pattern and power for believers’ future resurrection. Christ is the firstfruits and reigning Lord who will finally destroy death.

summary: Paul closes the letter with instructions about a collection for the Jerusalem believers, travel plans, and guidance regarding coworkers like Timothy and Apollos. He urges vigilance, steadfast faith, strength, and love, commends the household of Stephanas, and ends with greetings, a sober warning, and a prayerful cry, "Come, O Lord!"
main_themes: Generosity and relief for the saints

passage_divisions.title: The Collection for Jerusalem
Travel Plans and Coworkers
Standing Firm and Loving Well
Honor the Household of Stephanas
Final Greetings and Benediction

book_connection: Chapter 16 lands the pastoral and theological teaching of 1 Corinthians in practical steps—financial care, travel coordination, and honoring leaders—showing how love builds up the church. It ties the letter’s call to unity and holiness to everyday decisions and partnerships.
jesus_connection: The call to do everything in love flows from Jesus’ self-giving love at the cross. The prayer “Come, O Lord!” anchors the church’s generosity, service, and steadfastness in hope for Christ’s return.

summary: Paul greets the Corinthians and praises God as the source of all comfort, explaining how suffering and comfort flow through Christ for the church’s good. He recounts deadly hardships in Asia that taught him to rely on God who raises the dead, and he thanks the church for their prayers. Paul defends his integrity regarding changed travel plans, insisting his message and motives are rooted in God’s faithfulness, not fickleness. He closes by stressing that God has established them in Christ, sealing them with the Spirit, and that his restraint in not visiting was for their joy.

passage_divisions.title: Greeting to the church in Achaia
The God of all comfort
Delivered from deadly peril through prayer
Transparent conduct and mutual boasting in Christ
Not 'Yes and No'—God’s promises are 'Yes' in Christ
A restrained apostle: for your joy you stand by faith

book_connection: 2 Corinthians opens by framing Paul’s apostolic ministry through weakness, suffering, and God’s comfort, setting the tone for the letter’s defense of his integrity and his Christ-shaped leadership. This chapter lays the relational groundwork for later appeals, clarifying motives and highlighting the Spirit’s work among them.
jesus_connection: Paul anchors comfort, endurance, and every divine promise in Jesus: believers share in Christ’s sufferings and receive His overflowing comfort, and all God’s promises find their 'Yes' in Him. The Spirit given as a seal is Christ’s gift, tying present grace to future resurrection hope.

summary: Paul explains why he avoided another painful visit to Corinth and affirms his deep love expressed through a tearful letter. He urges the church to forgive and restore a disciplined offender, lest Satan exploit their severity. He recounts his restless travel from Troas to Macedonia when he could not find Titus. Paul concludes with a vivid picture of God leading him in Christ’s triumph, spreading the aroma of Christ, and contrasts sincere gospel ministry with peddling God’s word for profit.

passage_divisions.title: A Painful Letter from a Loving Heart
Discipline, Forgiveness, and Satan’s Schemes
No Rest in Troas; On to Macedonia
Led in Triumph; The Aroma of Christ; Sincere Ministry

book_connection: This chapter continues Paul’s defense of his pastoral decisions and his heart for reconciliation, setting up themes of comfort, integrity, and new-covenant ministry developed in chapters 3–7. It contrasts true apostolic sincerity with opponents who undercut Paul and commercialize ministry.
jesus_connection: Jesus is the victorious King who leads the triumphal procession and the source of the ‘aroma’ that brings life. Paul’s call to forgive mirrors Christ’s forgiveness, showing the gospel at work within the church.

summary: Paul defends his ministry by pointing to the Corinthians themselves as his living letter, written by the Spirit. He contrasts the old covenant carved on stone with the new covenant of the Spirit that gives life and surpassing glory. Using the veil over Moses’ face as an image, he explains how a spiritual veil remains until one turns to Christ. In Christ, the veil is removed, the Spirit brings freedom, and believers are transformed into the Lord’s image from glory to glory.

passage_divisions.title: Living Letters and New-Covenant Competence
The Surpassing Glory of the New Covenant
Veils Removed: Freedom and Transformation

book_connection: Second Corinthians defends Paul’s apostolic ministry and explains its God-given character. Chapter 3 grounds his defense in the new covenant ministry of the Spirit, preparing for chapters 4–6, where he describes suffering, hope, and reconciliation.
jesus_connection: Jesus inaugurates the new covenant through His death and resurrection, and pours out the Spirit who gives life and freedom. Turning to the Lord (Christ) removes the veil, enabling believers to behold and become like Him.

summary: Paul explains why he does not lose heart in ministry. He proclaims Christ openly, even though some are blinded to the gospel. God’s glory shines through fragile servants like clay jars, as sufferings display Jesus’ death and life. Fixing our eyes on the unseen, Paul calls present troubles “light and momentary” compared with the eternal weight of glory.

passage_divisions.title: Open Ministry, Veiled Gospel
Treasure in Jars of Clay
Faith Speaks and Spreads Grace
Eyes on the Unseen Glory

book_connection: This chapter continues Paul’s defense of his apostolic ministry (ch. 1–7), flowing from the new covenant glory in chapter 3 and moving toward hope of resurrection and new creation in chapters 5–6. It shows that weakness and suffering are not contradictions to the gospel, but the very means by which God’s power is revealed.
jesus_connection: Jesus is proclaimed as Lord, the image of God whose glory shines in our hearts. Paul’s sufferings mirror Jesus’ death so that Jesus’ life may be revealed, pointing to resurrection hope through Christ.

summary: Paul contrasts our mortal bodies with the eternal life God promises, assuring believers of the Spirit’s pledge and calling them to live by faith. He explains his ministry motives, grounded in the fear of the Lord and the compelling love of Christ. Through Jesus’ death and resurrection, God reconciles the world to Himself, making believers new creations and appointing them as ambassadors of reconciliation. The chapter climaxes with the gospel: Christ became sin for us so we might become God’s righteousness.
main_themes: Hope of resurrection and eternal life

passage_divisions.title: Earthly Tents and the Spirit’s Pledge
Faith, Presence, and Accountability
Ministry Motives: Fear of the Lord and Love of Christ
New Creation and the Ministry of Reconciliation

book_connection: This chapter continues Paul’s defense of his suffering yet Spirit-empowered ministry (chs. 3–6), showing how future hope and Christ’s love shape his present work. It deepens the letter’s emphasis on the new covenant and God’s power in human weakness.
jesus_connection: Jesus’ death and resurrection ground every claim in this chapter: our future hope, our present purpose, and our new identity. Paul explicitly centers the gospel in Christ’s substitution—He became sin so we might become God’s righteousness.

summary: Paul urges the Corinthians to respond to God’s grace now, defending the integrity of his ministry through a catalogue of hardships and Spirit-shaped virtues. He opens his heart to them and appeals for mutual affection. He then commands them not to be unequally yoked with unbelievers, grounding the call to separation in their identity as God’s temple. The chapter weaves urgency, authenticity, and holiness into one appeal.

passage_divisions.title: Now Is the Day of Salvation
Commending the Ministry Through Hardship and Holiness
Open Hearts, Mutual Affection
Do Not Be Unequally Yoked—You Are God’s Temple

book_connection: This chapter continues Paul’s defense of his apostolic ministry (begun in chs. 2–5) and his appeal for reconciliation. The command to be separate (6:14–18) frames holiness as essential to the new-covenant life Paul has just described (ch. 3) and prepares for renewed relationship in 7:2.
jesus_connection: Paul’s ministry shape—suffering yet powerful—mirrors the crucified and risen Christ. The call to holiness flows from union with Christ and the indwelling Spirit, through whom believers become God’s temple.

summary: Paul urges the Corinthians to pursue holiness in light of God’s promises, then opens his heart, describing hardship in Macedonia and the comfort God gave through Titus’s report. He explains the difference between godly sorrow that leads to repentance and life, and worldly sorrow that leads to death. The chapter closes with Paul’s joy over the Corinthians’ obedience and his renewed confidence in them.
main_themes: Holiness in response to God’s promises
Comfort from God through His people

passage_divisions.title: Holiness in Light of God’s Promises
Open Hearts and God’s Comfort in Affliction
Godly Sorrow Produces Repentance
Titus’s Joy and Paul’s Confidence Restored

book_connection: This chapter continues Paul’s effort to rebuild trust after conflict, tying back to his earlier explanations about suffering and comfort (1:3–7) and the ‘painful letter’ (2:1–11). It marks a turning point where the majority’s repentance brings renewed joy and unity between Paul and the church.
jesus_connection: Godly sorrow leads to repentance and salvation because Jesus’ death and resurrection open the way for true forgiveness and new life. The call to holiness reflects being set apart in Christ, whose Spirit empowers believers to cleanse themselves and grow in reverent obedience.

summary: Paul highlights the Macedonian churches’ stunning generosity amid affliction and poverty, urging the Corinthians to complete the relief offering they began. He grounds Christian giving in the grace of Christ, who became poor so believers might become rich. Paul also explains the safeguards and trusted coworkers handling the gift to ensure integrity before God and people.
main_themes: Equality within the body of Christ
important_people: Unnamed brother praised for the gospel

passage_divisions.title: Macedonia’s Grace-Fueled Generosity
An Appeal to Excel in Giving, Like Christ
Accountability in Handling the Gift
Commendation of the Team and Final Appeal

book_connection: Chapters 8–9 focus on the Jerusalem relief collection, showing how the gospel reshapes relationships, resources, and reputation. It follows renewed reconciliation (ch. 7) and precedes Paul’s defense against critics (chs. 10–13).
jesus_connection: Paul anchors generosity in Jesus’ self-giving: though rich, He became poor so believers might be made rich in grace. Christian giving reflects His incarnational descent and sacrificial love, not compulsion.

summary: Paul encourages the Corinthians to complete their promised gift for the Jerusalem believers, arranging for trusted brothers to ensure the offering is ready. He teaches the principle of generous sowing and cheerful giving, assuring them that God provides what is needed to do good. Their generosity will meet needs and overflow in thanksgiving to God, strengthening unity between churches. Paul ends by praising God for His indescribable gift.
main_themes: Thanksgiving and unity in the church

passage_divisions.title: Preparing the Promised Gift
The Principle of Sowing and Reaping
Generosity that Produces Thanksgiving
Doxology: God’s Indescribable Gift

book_connection: Chapters 8–9 form a unit on the collection for the saints, showing Paul’s pastoral care, financial integrity, and theology of grace. This chapter completes the appeal, grounding generosity in God’s abundant grace and the unity of the church.
jesus_connection: Generosity flows from the gospel: God has given His ‘indescribable gift’ in Christ (v.15). As Christ gave Himself (2 Corinthians 8:9), believers reflect Him by freely and joyfully giving to meet others’ needs.

summary: Paul appeals with Christlike gentleness while preparing to confront opponents who judge by worldly standards. He explains that true Christian ministry fights spiritual battles with God-given weapons, not worldly tactics. He defends his authority as given for building up the church, rejects self-commendation, and commits to boasting only in the Lord. Paul clarifies his God-assigned field of ministry and aims to preach beyond Corinth as their faith grows.

passage_divisions.title: Gentleness, Boldness, and Spiritual Warfare
Outward Appearances versus Real Authority
True Boasting and God-Given Boundaries

book_connection: Chapters 10–13 shift to a firmer defense of Paul’s ministry against critics in Corinth. This chapter sets the tone: Paul’s strength is Christlike, his authority is for edification, and his boast is in the Lord, themes that culminate in his later “fool’s speech” and his boasting in weakness (chs. 11–12).
jesus_connection: Paul appeals by the meekness and gentleness of Christ and wields authority given by the Lord. The pattern is Christlike: power expressed through humility, truth overcoming arguments, and boasting only in the Lord’s work.

summary: Paul defends his ministry against so-called “super-apostles,” expressing godly jealousy for the Corinthians’ pure devotion to Christ. He exposes false teachers who disguise themselves as righteous, contrasts their boasting with his own ‘foolish’ boasting, and lists his many sufferings as the true marks of an apostle. He insists on preaching free of charge to the Corinthians and concludes by boasting in weakness, recalling his humiliating escape from Damascus.
main_themes: True apostleship shown through weakness and suffering

passage_divisions.title: A Godly Jealousy and a Threat to Pure Devotion
Free-of-Charge Ministry and Unmasking False Apostles
‘Foolish’ Boasting and the Corinthians’ Tolerance of Abuse
Credentials of Suffering
Boasting in Weakness: The Damascus Escape

book_connection: This chapter continues Paul’s defense of his apostolic authenticity (chs. 10–13), contrasting worldly metrics of success with the cross-shaped pattern of ministry. It prepares for chapter 12’s climax on power perfected in weakness.
jesus_connection: Paul guards the church’s devotion to Christ as a pure bride and models Christlike, sacrificial leadership. His sufferings echo the pattern of the crucified Lord, showing that true gospel ministry bears the imprint of the cross.

summary: Paul reluctantly continues his 'boasting' to counter false apostles, recounting an unspeakable heavenly vision and then centering on his God-given 'thorn' that keeps him humble. He hears Christ’s word that grace is sufficient and power is perfected in weakness, so he boasts in weakness. Paul defends his apostleship through signs, perseverance, and financial integrity, reminding the Corinthians that he never exploited them. He prepares for a third visit, warning of unrepentant sin and pleading for their edification.

passage_divisions.title: Reluctant Boasting and the Heavenly Vision
The Thorn and Christ’s All-Sufficient Grace
Marks of a True Apostle and Financial Integrity
For Your Upbuilding: Fears, Repentance, and a Coming Visit

book_connection: This chapter crystallizes the letter’s message: Paul’s ministry is authenticated not by worldly strength but by weakness through which Christ’s power works. It also advances the travel plans and pastoral goals that run through 2 Corinthians, preparing the church for his imminent third visit and call to repentance.
jesus_connection: Christ personally speaks into Paul’s affliction, revealing the gospel pattern: divine power displayed through apparent weakness, just as the cross leads to resurrection power. Paul’s ministry, marked by suffering and integrity, mirrors Jesus’ self-giving love and servant leadership.

summary: Paul closes his letter with a firm warning and tender hope. He prepares the Corinthians for his third visit, urges them to test themselves in the faith, and explains that his authority aims to build them up, not tear them down. He calls the church to unity, peace, and mutual encouragement, and ends with a rich Trinitarian blessing.
main_themes: Unity and peace in the church

passage_divisions.title: Warning With Witnesses: Paul's Impending Visit
Examine Yourselves and Aim for Restoration
Final Exhortations and Trinitarian Blessing

book_connection: This chapter concludes Paul’s defense of his ministry (chs. 10–13) by pairing firm discipline with pastoral care. It seals the letter’s call to integrity, generosity, reconciliation, and weakness-as-strength with a prayer for unity and God’s presence.
jesus_connection: Paul points to Jesus’ crucifixion and resurrection as the pattern of power through weakness. The closing benediction names the grace of Jesus, the love of the Father, and the fellowship of the Spirit, centering the church’s life in the gospel and the Triune God.

summary: Luke opens Acts by recalling Jesus’ post-resurrection appearances and His command to wait in Jerusalem for the promised Holy Spirit. The disciples ask about the restoration of Israel, and Jesus redirects them to a global mission empowered by the Spirit. Jesus ascends, angels promise His return, and the disciples gather in prayer. Peter leads the community to replace Judas, and Matthias is chosen by lot.
main_themes: Promise and power of the Holy Spirit
Ascension and promised return of Jesus

passage_divisions.title: Prologue and the Promise of the Spirit
The Ascension and the Mission Mandate
Waiting in Prayer and Unity
Replacing Judas: Scripture and Leadership

book_connection: Acts 1 sets the blueprint for the book: the risen Jesus commissions Spirit-empowered witnesses who move from Jerusalem to Judea and Samaria and then to the ends of the earth. It also establishes apostolic leadership and the community’s posture of prayer and reliance on Scripture.
jesus_connection: Jesus is the risen, ascended Lord who sends the Spirit and defines the church’s mission. His ascension and promised return frame Acts as the ongoing work of the exalted Christ through His Spirit-empowered people.

summary: On Pentecost, the Holy Spirit is poured out on the gathered disciples, empowering them to speak in many languages. Peter explains the event as the fulfillment of Scripture, proclaims Jesus’ death and resurrection, and calls the crowd to repent and be baptized. About three thousand believe and are baptized. The chapter closes with a snapshot of the Spirit-formed community marked by teaching, fellowship, generosity, worship, and growth.
main_themes: Proclamation of Jesus as Lord and Messiah
Birth and life of the church

passage_divisions.title: Pentecost: The Spirit Comes
Peter Explains: Joel Fulfilled
Jesus Proclaimed as Lord and Christ
Cut to the Heart: Repentance and Baptism
The Spirit-Shaped Community

book_connection: Acts 2 delivers the promise of Acts 1:8: the Spirit empowers witness starting in Jerusalem. It launches the church’s mission and sets the template for gospel preaching, conversion, and community life throughout Acts.
jesus_connection: Peter announces that God raised and exalted Jesus, pouring out the Spirit from His throne. Jesus is revealed as both Lord and Messiah, the Savior whose name brings forgiveness, the promised gift of the Spirit, and the creation of a new people.

summary: Peter and John heal a man lame from birth at the temple gate called Beautiful. The crowd gathers in amazement, and Peter explains that Jesus is the source of the miracle, calling the people to repent so their sins may be wiped away and so they may share in the promised restoration.

passage_divisions.title: Healing at the Beautiful Gate
Peter Explains the Miracle
Call to Repentance and Fulfillment of the Prophets

book_connection: Acts 3 continues the pattern set in Acts 2: Spirit-empowered witness through signs and preaching in Jerusalem. It shows the apostles publicly proclaiming Jesus as the risen Messiah and calling Israel to repent, advancing the gospel’s spread from Jerusalem outward.
jesus_connection: Jesus is the crucified and risen Servant whose name heals and whose resurrection the apostles witness. Peter ties Jesus to the promised Prophet like Moses and to God’s blessing to Abraham, showing that salvation and restoration come through Him.

summary: Peter and John are arrested for preaching Jesus’ resurrection after healing a lame man. Before the Sanhedrin, Peter boldly proclaims that salvation is only in Jesus. The council threatens and releases them, and the church prays for boldness and is freshly filled with the Spirit. The chapter ends with radical generosity in the community, highlighting Barnabas as an example.
main_themes: The name of Jesus and salvation
Prayer and the Holy Spirit’s power
Unity and generosity in the church

passage_divisions.title: Arrest for Preaching the Resurrection
Peter Before the Sanhedrin
Command to Be Silent and Release
The Church Prays and Is Empowered
One Heart and Generous Hands

book_connection: Acts 4 advances the pattern promised in Acts 1:8—Spirit-empowered witness bringing growth despite opposition. It also deepens the portrait of the early church’s shared life begun in Acts 2.
jesus_connection: Jesus is proclaimed as crucified and risen, the rejected stone now the cornerstone, and the only name that saves. His ongoing work continues through the Spirit, empowering bold speech, healings, and a community shaped by his grace.

summary: Acts 5 contrasts deadly hypocrisy with unstoppable gospel power. Ananias and Sapphira lie about their gift and die, inspiring great fear. The apostles perform many healings, are arrested, miraculously freed, and boldly testify before the Sanhedrin. Gamaliel counsels restraint; the apostles are flogged yet rejoice and keep preaching Jesus.
main_themes: Holiness and integrity in the church
Obedience to God over human authority

passage_divisions.title: Ananias and Sapphira: The Fear of the Lord
Signs, Wonders, and Growing Crowds
Arrest and Angelic Release
Bold Witness Before the Sanhedrin
Gamaliel’s Counsel and the Apostles Flogged
Rejoicing and Relentless Teaching

book_connection: Acts 5 deepens the pattern begun in Acts 1–4: the risen Jesus advances His mission through the Spirit-empowered church despite internal threats and external opposition. The chapter also shows how the word spreads even as persecution intensifies.
jesus_connection: Peter centers the message on the crucified and exalted Jesus—Prince and Savior who grants repentance and forgiveness. The apostles’ joy in suffering mirrors Jesus’ own path, and the Spirit’s witness confirms that the risen Christ is actively leading His church.

summary: As the church grows in Jerusalem, a dispute arises because Greek-speaking widows are overlooked in the daily food distribution. The apostles lead the community to appoint seven Spirit-filled men to oversee this ministry, freeing the Twelve for prayer and the word. The church continues to expand, even many priests believe. Stephen, one of the seven, performs signs, faces opposition, and is falsely accused before the Sanhedrin as his face shines like an angel’s.

passage_divisions.title: Serving the Body: Seven Appointed
Stephen Opposed and Accused

book_connection: Acts 6 shows how the Spirit guides the church through internal challenges and external pressure, preserving unity and advancing the word. It prepares the way for Stephen’s speech (Acts 7) and the gospel’s spread beyond Jerusalem (Acts 8–12).
jesus_connection: The apostles imitate Jesus’ priorities: prayer, teaching, and compassionate care for the vulnerable. Stephen’s Spirit-empowered wisdom and radiant face anticipate Christlike witness in suffering, pointing to Jesus’ promise that the Spirit would give words and boldness before authorities.

summary: Stephen answers the Sanhedrin by retelling Israel’s story from Abraham to Solomon, highlighting God’s presence and guidance apart from any one land or building, and Israel’s repeated resistance to His messengers. He climaxes by accusing the leaders of resisting the Holy Spirit and betraying the Righteous One. As they rage, Stephen sees Jesus standing at God’s right hand and is stoned, praying for his killers. Saul witnesses the execution.
main_themes: God’s presence is not limited to place

passage_divisions.title: Stephen on Trial: Opening
Abraham and the Covenant
Joseph: God at Work in Exile
Moses: Early Life and Rejection
The Burning Bush and the Sent Deliverer
Idolatry in the Wilderness
Tabernacle, Temple, and the God Who Cannot Be Housed
Indictment: Resisting the Holy Spirit
Vision, Stoning, and Forgiveness

book_connection: Acts 7 closes the first major Jerusalem cycle: the gospel confronts Israel’s leaders, and persecution scatters the church (leading into Acts 8). Stephen’s speech reframes God’s mission as larger than the temple, preparing for the gospel’s spread beyond Jerusalem.
jesus_connection: Stephen declares Jesus as the exalted ‘Son of Man’ at God’s right hand, the promised ‘Righteous One’ foretold by the prophets. Moses’ promise of a prophet like himself finds its fulfillment in Jesus, whom the leaders have rejected.

summary: After Stephen’s death, persecution scatters believers beyond Jerusalem. Philip brings the gospel to Samaria with healings and exorcisms; Simon the sorcerer believes but is rebuked for trying to buy the Spirit’s power. Peter and John confirm the Samaritan believers, and then Philip is led to explain Isaiah 53 to an Ethiopian official, who believes and is baptized. The gospel advances across cultural and geographic boundaries with great joy.
main_themes: Power and gift of the Holy Spirit

passage_divisions.title: Persecution and Scattering
Philip Proclaims Christ in Samaria
Simon the Sorcerer and the Gift of the Spirit
Philip and the Ethiopian Eunuch

book_connection: Acts 8 shows Acts 1:8 unfolding: persecution propels the mission into Judea and Samaria, and the apostles confirm and guide the spread. It models how the word advances by the Spirit through witnesses, not despite opposition but often through it.
jesus_connection: Jesus promised the Spirit and a witness to Samaria and beyond; this chapter shows that promise being kept. Philip preaches Jesus from Isaiah 53, revealing Jesus as the suffering Servant whose death and resurrection bring salvation to the nations.

summary: Saul, a fierce persecutor of Christians, meets the risen Jesus on the road to Damascus and is radically converted, baptized, and commissioned. He begins preaching Jesus as the Son of God, faces plots to kill him, and is helped by Barnabas to be welcomed in Jerusalem. The church enjoys peace and growth, while Peter heals Aeneas in Lydda and raises Tabitha in Joppa, leading many to believe. The chapter pivots the story toward mission to the Gentiles and sets up Peter’s ministry along the coast.

passage_divisions.title: Saul Meets Jesus and Is Commissioned
Early Preaching and Escape from Damascus
Barnabas Advocates for Saul; Church Strengthened
Peter Heals Aeneas at Lydda
Peter Raises Tabitha at Joppa

book_connection: Acts 9 is a hinge: Saul’s conversion introduces the future apostle to the Gentiles, and Peter’s coastal ministry prepares for the Gentile breakthrough in Acts 10. The church’s growth and the Spirit’s guidance continue Luke’s theme from Acts 1:8.
jesus_connection: The risen Jesus personally confronts and commissions Saul, showing that He leads the church’s mission. The healings and the raising of Tabitha show Jesus’ ongoing power working through His servants and His compassion for the weak.

summary: God orchestrates a meeting between Cornelius, a Gentile centurion, and Peter through visions. Peter learns not to call people unclean, preaches Jesus as Lord of all, and the Holy Spirit falls on the Gentiles. They speak in tongues, are baptized, and the church recognizes God’s welcome to the nations.
main_themes: Baptism and the gift of the Spirit

passage_divisions.title: Cornelius’s Vision and Sending
Peter’s Vision and the Spirit’s Guidance
Peter Meets Cornelius
Peter’s Gospel Message
The Spirit Falls and Baptism Follows

book_connection: Acts 10 is a turning point where the gospel crosses decisively into Gentile territory, fulfilling Acts 1:8. It sets up Peter’s defense in Acts 11 and paves the way for the Jerusalem Council in Acts 15.
jesus_connection: Peter proclaims Jesus as Lord of all who was anointed by the Spirit, crucified, raised, and appointed Judge. Forgiveness in Jesus’ name is offered to everyone who believes, and the risen Christ pours out the Spirit on Gentiles just as at Pentecost.

summary: Peter defends his visit to Cornelius by recounting God’s vision and the Holy Spirit’s work, convincing the Jerusalem believers that Gentiles are included in salvation. The gospel then spreads in Antioch, where Barnabas and Saul teach a growing church and the disciples are first called Christians. Prophets foretell a famine, prompting the Antioch church to send relief to believers in Judea.
main_themes: The Holy Spirit’s guidance and validation
Mission expansion from Jerusalem to the nations
Generosity and unity across the church

passage_divisions.title: Peter Defends God’s Work Among the Gentiles
The Gospel Takes Root in Antioch
Prophecy and Practical Love

book_connection: Acts 11 marks a turning point: the church recognizes God’s direct inclusion of Gentiles and Antioch emerges as a mission hub. This prepares the way for Paul’s journeys and the later Jerusalem Council (Acts 15).
jesus_connection: Jesus promised Spirit-baptism and a mission to all nations; Acts 11 shows both happening through Him. Repentance unto life is granted in His name, revealing Jesus as Lord of all, not of one ethnicity.

summary: Herod Agrippa I kills James and imprisons Peter during the Feast of Unleavened Bread, but God miraculously frees Peter in answer to the church’s prayers. Peter reports his deliverance and goes into hiding, while Herod executes the guards and later receives divine judgment for accepting worship. Despite opposition, the word of God grows, and Barnabas and Saul return from Jerusalem with John Mark.
main_themes: The unstoppable spread of the gospel
important_people: Mary the mother of John Mark

passage_divisions.title: Persecution Strikes; the Church Prays
Peter Rescued by an Angel
Herod’s Rage and Judgment
The Word Advances; Team Transitions

book_connection: Acts 12 closes the Jerusalem-focused section by showing God’s protection of His witnesses and the removal of a hostile ruler, paving the way for the Gentile mission that follows in Acts 13. It contrasts human opposition with the Spirit-empowered advance of the word.
jesus_connection: Jesus promised persecution and deliverance for His witnesses and the Spirit’s power for mission; Acts 12 displays both. The Lord who frees Peter and judges Herod is the risen Jesus ruling His church, ensuring the gospel continues to spread.

summary: The church in Antioch, guided by the Holy Spirit, commissions Barnabas and Saul for mission. They evangelize Cyprus, confront a sorcerer, and the proconsul believes. In Pisidian Antioch, Paul preaches a sweeping sermon showing Jesus as the fulfillment of God’s promises, proclaiming forgiveness and justification by faith. Strong mixed responses follow: many believe, others oppose, so Paul and Barnabas turn openly to the Gentiles as the word spreads.
main_themes: Justification by faith, not the law

passage_divisions.title: Commissioned by the Spirit at Antioch
Cyprus: Power Encounter and a Proconsul’s Faith
Journey to Pisidian Antioch; John Mark Departs
Paul’s Sermon: Promise to Fulfillment (Part 1)
Paul’s Sermon: Death, Resurrection, and Justification (Part 2)
Division, Turning to the Gentiles, and Joy in the Spirit

book_connection: Acts 13 launches Paul’s first missionary journey and marks the shift from a Jerusalem-centered story to a Gentile mission shaped by the Spirit. It sets the pattern of synagogue-first preaching, scriptural proof, mixed response, and ongoing expansion to new regions.
jesus_connection: Paul proclaims Jesus as the promised Son, crucified and raised, whose resurrection fulfills Scripture and secures forgiveness and justification. The chapter centers on Jesus’ lordship and living power, which both saves and divides, as the gospel moves toward the nations.

summary: Paul and Barnabas preach in Iconium, face fierce opposition, and move on to Lystra where a healing leads the crowd to mistake them for gods. They refuse worship, proclaim the living Creator, but Paul is stoned and left for dead—then rises and continues the mission to Derbe. Returning through the same cities, they strengthen the new believers, appoint elders, and finally report back in Antioch how God opened the door of faith to the Gentiles.
main_themes: Turning from idols to the living God
God’s grace confirmed by signs and wonders
important_people: Hostile Jews from Antioch and Iconium

passage_divisions.title: Bold witness and division in Iconium
Healing at Lystra and the crowd’s idolatry
Paul stoned, yet mission continues
Strengthening churches and appointing elders
Reporting God’s work to Antioch

book_connection: Acts 14 completes Paul and Barnabas’s first missionary journey, showing the gospel taking root in Gentile regions and churches being organized with elders. It sets the stage for the Jerusalem Council in Acts 15 by highlighting Gentile conversion without becoming Jewish.
jesus_connection: The risen Jesus continues His mission through His witnesses, confirming the message of grace by signs and sustaining them through suffering. Paul’s rejection, perseverance, and call to turn from idols echo Jesus’ call to repent and follow the living God.

summary: A dispute breaks out when some teach that Gentile believers must be circumcised to be saved. Paul and Barnabas go to Jerusalem where the apostles and elders, after testimonies from Peter, Paul, Barnabas, and a judgment by James, affirm salvation by grace and set a few necessary guidelines for Gentile believers. A letter carrying this decision brings joy to Antioch. Later, Paul and Barnabas separate over John Mark and launch separate ministry teams.
main_themes: Salvation by grace, not by the law
Unity of the church across cultures
Guidance by the Holy Spirit in church decisions
Freedom with love for others’ consciences

passage_divisions.title: The Dispute over Circumcision
The Jerusalem Council Deliberates
The Council’s Letter and Antioch’s Joy
Paul and Barnabas Part Ways

book_connection: Acts 15 is the hinge that secures the Gentile mission within the one church. It clarifies the gospel and paves the way for the second missionary journey and the spread of the gospel to new regions.
jesus_connection: The council affirms that people are saved by the grace of the Lord Jesus, not by works of the law—echoing Jesus’ finished work. James’s use of the prophets shows that Jesus’ Davidic restoration opens God’s people to the nations.

summary: Paul recruits Timothy and, guided by the Spirit, carries the mission into Macedonia. In Philippi, Lydia and then the jailer with his household believe and are baptized. A delivered slave girl’s owners instigate a mob, leading to Paul and Silas being beaten and imprisoned, yet God frees them through an earthquake. The chapter ends with a public apology from the magistrates and strengthening of the new church.

passage_divisions.title: Timothy Joins and Churches Strengthened
The Macedonian Call: Guided by the Spirit
Lydia’s Conversion in Philippi
Deliverance, Backlash, and Imprisonment
Midnight Praise and the Jailer’s Salvation
Public Vindication and Encouragement of the Church

book_connection: Acts 16 marks a pivotal westward turn of the gospel into Macedonia and establishes Philippi as a key base. It continues Luke’s pattern of church planting through Spirit-led guidance, opposition, and surprising conversions.
jesus_connection: Jesus, the risen Lord, continues directing His mission by His Spirit and freeing people from sin and demonic power. The message of salvation by believing in the Lord Jesus (16:31) echoes the core gospel of Christ’s death and resurrection for all peoples.

summary: Paul and Silas preach in Thessalonica, where some believe but opposition forces them to leave. In Berea the Jews carefully examine the Scriptures and many believe, but opponents from Thessalonica stir trouble again. Paul is taken to Athens, where he addresses philosophers at the Areopagus, proclaiming the Creator God, the call to repent, and Jesus’ resurrection. Responses range from mockery to sincere belief.
main_themes: Repentance and final judgment through the risen Jesus

passage_divisions.title: Reasoning in Thessalonica and Rising Opposition
The Noble Bereans and Renewed Agitation
Paul’s Distress in Athens and Public Debates
The Areopagus Address: The Known God
Mixed Responses to the Resurrection

book_connection: Acts 17 shows the gospel advancing into major Macedonian and Greek centers, with a repeated pattern: synagogue reasoning, mixed reception, persecution, and mission agility. It culminates in Paul’s model of addressing a pagan audience without Scripture citations yet still proclaiming creation, repentance, judgment, and the resurrection.
jesus_connection: Paul proclaims that Jesus is the promised Christ who suffered, rose, and is appointed by God as the righteous Judge. The resurrection is God’s public confirmation of Jesus’ identity and the basis for a universal call to repentance.

summary: Paul leaves Athens for Corinth, works with Aquila and Priscilla, and plants a strong church amid opposition. Encouraged by the Lord in a vision, he stays 18 months. A legal challenge before Gallio fails, giving the mission breathing room. After traveling through Ephesus, Jerusalem, and Antioch, the chapter closes with Apollos’ refined ministry powerfully proving from Scripture that Jesus is the Christ.

passage_divisions.title: Arrival in Corinth: Tentmaking and Firstfruits
Do Not Be Afraid: The Lord’s Vision in Corinth
Before Gallio’s Tribunal
Transitions: Vow, Ephesus Visit, and Strengthening Churches
Apollos: Eloquence Refined by Discipleship

book_connection: Acts 18 advances Paul’s second missionary journey into the strategic hub of Corinth and sets up the third journey through Ephesus. It shows the gospel’s spread through cities, courts, households, and partnerships, highlighting God’s guidance and the Spirit’s power.
jesus_connection: Jesus directly encourages Paul to keep speaking, promising His presence and protection. Apollos’ ministry shows how the Scriptures point to Jesus as the Christ, and how the risen Lord continues building His church through gifted, teachable servants.

summary: Paul arrives in Ephesus, instructs disciples of John, and they receive the Holy Spirit. He then teaches for two years, God works unusual miracles, and many turn from occult practices. A silversmith named Demetrius stirs a riot over lost idol trade, but the city clerk quiets the crowd and insists legal channels be used. The word of the Lord spreads powerfully despite opposition.
main_themes: The Holy Spirit’s work in believers
Power of Jesus’ name over evil
Repentance from idolatry and occult practices
Gospel growth amid civic and economic opposition

passage_divisions.title: Disciples of John Receive the Holy Spirit
Reasoning Daily and the Word Spreads
Unusual Miracles and the Defeat of Magic
Paul’s Travel Resolve
The Ephesian Riot over Artemis

book_connection: Acts 19 shows the gospel’s advance into a major urban and spiritual center (Ephesus) and models how the Way challenges religious, social, and economic structures. It prepares the transition from Paul’s long Ephesian ministry to his journey toward Jerusalem and eventually Rome.
jesus_connection: Jesus pours out the Holy Spirit on believers, and his name exercises authority over evil powers. The chapter displays the risen Lord extending his kingdom through word and Spirit, rescuing people from idols to serve the living God.

summary: Paul travels through Macedonia and Greece, strengthening believers, then heads to Troas where God raises Eutychus after a fatal fall. Pressing on to Miletus, Paul summons the Ephesian elders and delivers a moving farewell: recounting his ministry, warning of false teachers, charging them to shepherd God’s flock, and commending them to God’s grace. The chapter ends with tearful prayer and parting as Paul hurries toward Jerusalem.
main_themes: Generosity and hard work for the weak
The church purchased by Christ’s blood

passage_divisions.title: Through Macedonia and Greece
Eutychus Raised at Troas
Moving South to Miletus
Paul’s Testimony to the Elders
Charge: Shepherd God’s Blood-Bought Church
Tearful Farewell and Departure

book_connection: Acts 20 pivots from Paul’s fruitful third journey to his determined march toward Jerusalem and eventual trials. Luke highlights Spirit-led travel, church strengthening, and leadership handover—key threads in Acts’ story of the gospel advancing despite opposition.
jesus_connection: Paul centers everything on the gospel of God’s grace and the church purchased by Jesus’ blood. The Lord’s saying, "It is more blessed to give than to receive," echoes Jesus’ kingdom ethic and shapes Christian leadership and community life.

summary: Paul sails to the Levant, is warned by believers through the Spirit about danger in Jerusalem, yet resolutely continues. In Jerusalem he reports Gentile mission successes, takes part in a purification plan to calm rumors, but is falsely accused of defiling the temple. A riot erupts; Roman soldiers rescue and arrest Paul. On the steps of the barracks, Paul secures permission to address the crowd.
main_themes: Jew–Gentile tensions and unity in the church

passage_divisions.title: From Miletus to Tyre: Prayerful Farewells
At Caesarea: Prophecy and Resolve
Jerusalem Meeting: Rumors and a Purification Plan
Riot in the Temple and Roman Intervention
Permission to Speak

book_connection: Acts 21 marks the pivot from Paul’s missionary travels to his arrests and trials, fulfilling earlier hints that he would suffer for Christ. Luke shows the gospel advancing even through legal processes and public speeches before both Jewish and Roman authorities.
jesus_connection: Paul’s determined journey to Jerusalem echoes Jesus’ own set face toward the city and His willing embrace of suffering. The chapter highlights witness through hardship, pointing to the gospel pattern: life comes through faithful suffering and God’s sovereign care.

summary: Paul addresses a hostile Jerusalem crowd in Hebrew, recounting his Jewish upbringing, his persecution of Christians, and his encounter with Jesus on the road to Damascus. He describes his commissioning through Ananias and a later temple vision that sent him to the Gentiles. The crowd erupts when he mentions Gentiles, leading the Roman commander to detain him. Paul invokes his Roman citizenship to avoid flogging, and the commander convenes the Sanhedrin to learn the charges.

passage_divisions.title: Paul’s Jewish Credentials and Zeal
The Damascus Road and Ananias’ Commission
Vision in the Temple: Sent to the Gentiles
Riot Rekindled and Roman Intervention
Protected by Citizenship
Toward the Sanhedrin

book_connection: Acts 22 continues Luke’s pattern of showing the gospel defended before Jewish and Roman authorities and highlights Paul’s repeated conversion testimony as a defense of the Way. It advances the narrative toward Rome by placing Paul under Roman protection and legal process.
jesus_connection: The risen Jesus directly confronts and commissions Paul, identifying Himself as the persecuted Lord and the Righteous One. Paul’s mission to the Gentiles flows from Jesus’ saving purposes for all nations.

summary: Paul faces the Sanhedrin, clashes with the high priest, and shrewdly highlights the resurrection, dividing Pharisees and Sadducees. That night the Lord encourages Paul, promising he will testify in Rome. A murder plot arises but is uncovered by Paul’s nephew, leading the Roman commander to transfer Paul safely to Caesarea with a formal letter to Governor Felix.
main_themes: The resurrection as the heart of the gospel

passage_divisions.title: Paul Before the Sanhedrin: Conscience and Rebuke
Resurrection at the Center: Dividing the Council
Night Vision: Courage for Rome
The Assassination Plot and a Nephew’s Courage
Escort to Caesarea and the Commander’s Letter

book_connection: Acts 23 advances the transition from Paul’s Jerusalem turmoil to his formal trials under Roman authority, setting the path toward Rome. It shows God using both Jewish councils and Roman officials to move His witness forward.
jesus_connection: The risen Jesus personally strengthens Paul and directs his mission, echoing how God vindicated Jesus after unjust trials. Paul’s focus on the resurrection centers the gospel: Jesus’ victory over death guarantees the hope Paul proclaims.

summary: Paul stands trial before Governor Felix in Caesarea. The high priest’s lawyer, Tertullus, accuses Paul of being a troublemaker and desecrating the temple. Paul defends himself, affirming his loyalty to the God of Israel, the Law and the Prophets, and the hope of the resurrection. Felix delays judgment, keeps Paul under light guard, listens to the gospel, but seeks a bribe and leaves Paul imprisoned for two years.

passage_divisions.title: Charges Brought Before Felix
Paul’s Defense: The Way and the Resurrection
Felix Delays the Case
Felix Listens but Refuses to Repent

book_connection: Acts 24 continues Luke’s theme of the gospel advancing through trials. Paul’s hearings before Roman officials show that Christianity is not a political threat, while God uses these moments to spread the message toward Rome.
jesus_connection: Paul testifies to faith in Christ and the coming judgment, echoing Jesus’ teaching on resurrection and accountability. Jesus’ promise that his witnesses would testify before governors is fulfilled as Paul speaks courageously before Felix.

summary: Festus, the new Roman governor, inherits Paul’s case and refuses a Jewish plot to move Paul to Jerusalem. After an unprovable set of accusations, Paul asserts his innocence and appeals to Caesar. King Agrippa II and Bernice visit, and Festus lays out the dilemma: the dispute centers on Jesus, whom Paul claims is alive. Agrippa agrees to hear Paul, setting up the next chapter’s defense.

passage_divisions.title: Festus Takes Office; Plot Resurfaces
Hearing in Caesarea and Appeal to Caesar
Festus Consults Agrippa
Paul Presented with Pomp; The Real Issue Stated

book_connection: Acts 25 advances the movement of the gospel from Jerusalem toward Rome through Paul’s legal journey. The chapter shows how God uses Roman processes and Gentile rulers to carry the message to kings, fulfilling Jesus’ mission trajectory in Acts 1:8.
jesus_connection: At the heart of the case is Jesus’ resurrection: Paul insists Jesus is alive. The chapter highlights that Christianity is not merely a moral code or sectarian dispute but a claim about the risen Lord, which drives the church’s witness before rulers.

summary: Paul gives his defense before King Agrippa, recounting his life as a Pharisee, his violent persecution of Christians, and his encounter with the risen Jesus on the road to Damascus. He explains his commission to preach repentance and light to Jews and Gentiles, grounding it in Moses and the prophets. Festus calls Paul insane, but Paul appeals to Agrippa’s knowledge of these public events. Agrippa admits Paul has done nothing worthy of death or prison, yet notes Paul would have been freed if he had not appealed to Caesar.

passage_divisions.title: Permission to Speak and Respectful Appeal
Paul’s Former Life as a Pharisee and Persecutor
The Damascus Road Revelation and Commission
Obedience to the Vision and the Scriptural Hope
Festus Interrupts; Agrippa Confronted; Verdict Rendered

book_connection: Acts repeatedly shows the gospel advancing through witness, suffering, and Spirit-empowered testimony before both commoners and rulers. Chapter 26 climaxes Paul’s defenses, linking his mission to Israel’s Scriptures and setting up his journey to Rome.
jesus_connection: Jesus personally appears to Paul and commissions him, making the risen Christ the source and center of the mission. The chapter proclaims Jesus as the suffering and risen Messiah who brings light and forgiveness to Jews and Gentiles.

summary: Paul is sent to Italy by sea under a centurion named Julius. Despite Paul’s warning, the ship sails late in the season, is caught in a violent northeaster, and drifts for two weeks. An angel assures Paul that all aboard will live though the ship will be lost. The ship runs aground and breaks apart, yet every person reaches shore safely.

passage_divisions.title: Setting Sail to Italy
Ignoring Wise Counsel
The Great Storm and Lost Hope
A Word from God: Courage and Promise
Near Land: Tested Obedience
Breaking Bread, Breaking Ship—All Saved

book_connection: Acts 27 shows God advancing the gospel to Rome through trials. It highlights Paul’s Spirit-empowered witness and God’s sovereign guidance despite opposition and hardship.
jesus_connection: Paul’s calm leadership and promise of life in the storm echo Jesus’ lordship over wind and waves and His presence with His people. The shared meal and thanksgiving hint at Jesus’ provision and the hope that sustains the church in crisis.

summary: After surviving shipwreck, Paul and his companions are shown unusual kindness on Malta, where God authenticates Paul’s message through protection from a viper and many healings. After wintering there, they travel to Italy and finally reach Rome, where Paul meets local believers and then addresses the Jewish leaders. Some are persuaded by his teaching about Jesus from the Law and Prophets, others are not; Paul cites Isaiah to explain this mixed response and announces that salvation is also for the Gentiles. The book closes with Paul under house arrest in Rome, boldly proclaiming the kingdom of God for two years.
main_themes: The unstoppable spread of the gospel to the nations
The kingdom of God proclaimed with boldness
Hospitality and Christian fellowship on the journey

passage_divisions.title: Kindness and Power on Malta
Final Steps to Rome
Paul and the Jewish Leaders in Rome
Isaiah’s Verdict and an Open-Ended Mission

book_connection: Acts 28 fulfills the trajectory of Acts 1:8: the gospel moves from Jerusalem to Judea and Samaria and finally to the heart of the empire, Rome. The open-ended conclusion invites readers to see the mission continuing beyond Paul and beyond the book.
jesus_connection: Paul proclaims the kingdom of God and teaches about the Lord Jesus, continuing Jesus’ own mission and message. The healings and bold witness echo Jesus’ ministry and show the risen Christ still at work through his servants.

summary: Luke opens with a careful prologue to Theophilus, then records two angelic announcements: John the Baptist’s birth to Zechariah and Elizabeth, and Jesus’ birth to Mary. Mary visits Elizabeth; John leaps in the womb and Mary sings the Magnificat. John is born and named; Zechariah’s speech returns and he prophesies the Benedictus. The chapter closes with John growing in the wilderness, awaiting his public ministry.
main_themes: Reversal for the humble and mercy for the lowly
From doubt to faith and joyful praise

book_connection: Luke begins by grounding his Gospel in eyewitness testimony to give certainty. Chapter 1 sets the pattern of promise and fulfillment, the work of the Spirit, joy, and salvation history that Luke will trace through Jesus’ ministry and, in Acts, through the early church.
jesus_connection: This chapter directly introduces Jesus as the Son of the Most High, the promised Davidic king, conceived by the Holy Spirit. John’s birth and calling show that Jesus’ coming is God’s long-prepared rescue for his people.

summary: Luke 2 narrates Jesus’ birth in Bethlehem, angelic announcement to shepherds, and the shepherds’ visit and praise. Jesus is presented at the temple, where Simeon and Anna testify that He is God’s salvation for Israel and the nations. The family returns to Nazareth, and Jesus grows in wisdom and grace. At age twelve, He stays in the temple, revealing His unique relationship to the Father before returning home in obedience.

book_connection: Luke emphasizes God’s salvation plan unfolding from humble beginnings to worldwide scope, with Jerusalem and the temple as key settings. This chapter establishes eyewitness testimony and the Spirit-led recognition of Jesus that Luke will continue to highlight.
jesus_connection: Here Jesus is revealed as Savior, Christ, and Lord—God’s light for the Gentiles and glory for Israel. His humble birth, obedience under the Law, and awareness of His Father’s will point to the gospel: God’s Son entered our world to bring peace and redemption.

summary: John the Baptist appears in the Jordan region calling Israel to repent and be baptized, fulfilling Isaiah’s prophecy of preparing the Lord’s way. He urges practical righteousness, denies being the Christ, and warns of coming judgment. Jesus is baptized, the Spirit descends on Him, and the Father’s voice affirms Him as the beloved Son. Luke then traces Jesus’ genealogy back to Adam, signaling salvation for all humanity.
main_themes: Jesus’ divine Sonship and anointing by the Spirit

passage_divisions.title: John’s Call and Isaiah’s Voice
Fruit of Repentance
The Coming One and the Winnowing
Jesus’ Baptism: Son and Spirit
The Genealogy to Adam

book_connection: Luke moves from Jesus’ birth narratives to the launch of His public ministry. John’s preparatory work and Jesus’ baptism introduce the Spirit-empowered mission that Luke will unfold, while the genealogy back to Adam fits Luke’s emphasis on salvation for all people.
jesus_connection: Jesus is revealed as God’s beloved Son and anointed by the Spirit, confirming His identity and mission. The genealogy frames Him as the true Son of David and Son of Adam, the representative who brings God’s salvation to all humanity.

summary: Jesus, full of the Spirit, resists the devil’s temptations in the wilderness. Returning to Galilee, He announces His mission by reading Isaiah in Nazareth but is rejected by His hometown. In Capernaum He teaches with authority, drives out a demon, heals many—including Simon’s mother-in-law—and prioritizes preaching the kingdom of God in other towns. News about Him spreads widely.
main_themes: Good news to the poor and oppressed

passage_divisions.title: The Temptation in the Wilderness
Jesus Announces His Mission in Nazareth
Hometown Rejection
Authority in Capernaum’s Synagogue
Healings in Capernaum and Mission Priority

book_connection: Luke highlights Jesus’ Spirit-empowered mission, His concern for the marginalized, and His universal reach beyond Israel. Luke 4 serves as a programmatic chapter: it unveils Jesus’ identity, message, and the pattern of response—astonishment, opposition, and spreading fame.
jesus_connection: This chapter presents Jesus as the Spirit-anointed Messiah who proclaims and embodies God’s kingdom. His victory over temptation, authoritative teaching, and compassionate healings reveal who He is and why He came.

summary: Jesus calls fishermen through a miraculous catch, cleanses a man with leprosy, forgives and heals a paralytic, calls Levi the tax collector, and teaches about fasting with images of the bridegroom and new wine. The chapter highlights Jesus' authority, compassion, and the newness of His mission. Crowds grow, opposition begins, and disciples start leaving everything to follow Him.
main_themes: Jesus' authority to teach, heal, and forgive

Levi's Call and the Banquet with Sinners

book_connection: Luke emphasizes Jesus' Spirit-empowered ministry to the poor, sinners, and outsiders, and His authority over sickness, sin, and Sabbath traditions. Chapter 5 advances these themes by showing early disciple-calling, rising opposition, and the arrival of something new in Jesus' mission.
jesus_connection: This chapter centers on Jesus Himself: His authority to forgive sins, cleanse the unclean, call disciples, and inaugurate the new era of the kingdom. The bridegroom and new wine imagery points to Jesus as the focal point of God’s new covenant work.

summary: Jesus confronts Sabbath controversies, heals a man with a withered hand, and chooses the Twelve after a night of prayer. He then teaches on a level place, pronouncing blessings and woes and calling disciples to enemy-love, generous mercy, integrity, and obedience that endures the storms of life.
main_themes: Love of enemies and generous grace
important_people: Crowds from Judea, Jerusalem, Tyre, Sidon

book_connection: Luke 6 intensifies conflict with religious leaders, establishes the Twelve as the renewed people of God, and lays out core disciple-ethics. It parallels Matthew’s Sermon on the Mount, but in Luke it roots the kingdom’s upside-down values in Jesus’ merciful authority and mission to all.
jesus_connection: Jesus reveals himself as Lord of the Sabbath, compassionate healer, and authoritative teacher whose words demand obedience. His ethic of enemy-love and mercy discloses the Father’s character and the shape of life in God’s kingdom.

summary: Jesus heals a centurion’s servant from a distance, raises a widow’s only son at Nain, answers John the Baptist’s question by pointing to messianic works, and defends John while critiquing a fickle generation. In a Pharisee’s home, a sinful woman’s love displays the fruit of forgiveness, and Jesus declares her forgiven and saved by faith.
main_themes: Jesus’ authority over sickness, death, and sin
important_people: The widow of Nain and her son

book_connection: Luke highlights Jesus’ compassion and authority, especially toward outsiders, and shows Him fulfilling Israel’s story and the prophets. This chapter advances Luke’s themes of reversal, table fellowship, and the call to faith, anticipating the gospel’s spread to all peoples.
jesus_connection: Here Jesus reveals Himself as the merciful Messiah who fulfills Scripture, commands life, and forgives sins. His authority and compassion invite humble faith and foreshadow the cross where forgiveness is secured.

summary: Jesus proclaims the kingdom, supported by women disciples, and teaches how people receive God’s word. He displays authority over nature, demons, disease, and death, calling for true hearing and persevering faith. The chapter climaxes with the calming of a storm, the deliverance of a man called Legion, the healing of a bleeding woman, and the raising of Jairus’s daughter.
main_themes: Hearing and responding to God’s word
Jesus’ authority over nature, demons, disease, and death

book_connection: Luke highlights Jesus’ compassion and authority that bring salvation to outsiders and insiders alike. This chapter deepens the theme of hearing the word rightly and shows the kingdom’s power breaking in through Jesus’ deeds.
jesus_connection: This chapter centers on Jesus as the sower of God’s word and the Lord over chaos, demons, disease, and death. His identity is revealed through His words and works, inviting faith-filled hearing and obedience.

summary: Jesus empowers the Twelve for mission, feeds a vast crowd, and reveals His identity as the Christ who must suffer. He is transfigured in glory, heals a tormented boy, teaches true greatness and kingdom partnership, and resolutely sets His face toward Jerusalem while calling followers to costly discipleship.
main_themes: Discipleship and the cost of following

book_connection: Luke 9 is a turning point: Jesus is revealed as the Christ, teaches the necessity of His suffering, and in 9:51 sets His face toward Jerusalem, launching the long journey to the cross that dominates the rest of Luke.
jesus_connection: This chapter directly centers on Jesus—His authority, identity, compassion, glory, and mission to suffer and rise. It clarifies the gospel: the Christ must suffer, and His followers walk the same path of self-denial and faithful trust.

summary: Jesus sends seventy-two disciples ahead with urgent instructions and a message of peace and healing. He pronounces woes on unrepentant towns, celebrates the Father’s revelation to the humble, and reorients the disciples’ joy to heaven’s record. He then teaches love of neighbor through the Good Samaritan and models true discipleship priority with Mary and Martha.
main_themes: Reception and rejection of the gospel

book_connection: Luke’s travel narrative (9:51–19:27) shows Jesus moving toward Jerusalem while forming disciples. Chapter 10 deepens this by expanding mission beyond the Twelve, clarifying responses to Jesus, and defining neighbor-love and attentive discipleship.
jesus_connection: Jesus is the Lord of the harvest who sends, the King whose nearness signals God’s kingdom, and the Son who uniquely reveals the Father. His teaching and example reorient power, mercy, and priorities around Himself and His gospel.

summary: Jesus teaches a model prayer, urges bold perseverance in asking God, and promises the gift of the Holy Spirit. He defeats a mute demon, refutes accusations of working by Beelzebul, and warns about empty religiosity and inner darkness. As crowds seek signs, He points to Jonah and the Queen of the South and then pronounces woes on Pharisees and law experts for hypocrisy and burdening others. The chapter ends with rising hostility toward Him.
main_themes: The Holy Spirit as God's good gift
True blessedness in hearing and obeying
important_people: A mute man delivered from a demon
